problem: Learned potential-based reward shaping via GCN reward propagation (Klissarov & Precup) uses a plain GCN, whose aggregation may not be the best fit for trajectory-graph data. Sparse-reward 3D navigation POMDPs remain hard for PPO.
motivation: In 3D navigation the agent typically gets only a visual observation and a single reward at episode end, which slows RL convergence. Choosing a GNN architecture suited to the sequential trajectory graphs and to identifying important transitions should improve the learned shaping function.
key_idea: Replace the GCN in graph-based reward propagation with GAT (attention over transitions) or GraphSAGE (mean + LSTM aggregators) to learn better potential functions for reward shaping.
insight: Architecture choice for the shaping GNN matters: on the harder MazeS3, GAT reaches 76.56 vs 66.96 for GCN and 59.75 for PPO, while on FourRooms all methods are similar (differences within std). GAT attention concentrates on trajectory start, pre-goal transitions and the moment the goal enters the field of view without any supervision, giving interpretability. Evidence is limited: only learning curves and one final-performance table, with no seed count and large std.
method: Reward propagation framework: states are nodes, transitions from sampled trajectories form linear graphs; the GNN output is a potential Phi used for potential-based shaping F=gamma*Phi(s')-Phi(s)
Loss: cross-entropy on base-case states (first/last states and non-zero reward states) plus eta=10 times a Laplacian message-passing smoothness term
Phi_GAT: two-layer GAT, 64 hidden units, 4 attention heads in first layer, LeakyReLU; attention scores are interpretable
Phi_GraphSAGE: two-layer, mean aggregator with ReLU in first layer, LSTM aggregator in second layer to exploit sequential data
Policy: PPO actor-critic with 3-layer CNN encoder (32/64/32 filters); GNN node features are CNN encoder outputs; 16 parallel envs, 128-step rollouts, GNN updated at episode end
Complexity: sparse aggregation keeps forward pass linear in nodes, comparable to GCN baseline

setting.backbone: PPO actor-critic with CNN encoder + GAT/GraphSAGE reward-shaping network (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Online RL interaction only: 5M steps on FourRooms, 20M steps on MazeS3; no extra data
setting.action_space: discrete: move forward, turn left, turn right

numbers.extra: 5M training steps; reward scaled to [0,100]; mean ± std; not a standard nav benchmark
numbers.evidence: Table 2: Final performance for both environments, Phi_GAT 69.93 ± 5.72

numbers.extra: 20M training steps; reward scaled to [0,100]; mean ± std

numbers_note: Learning curves are only in figures; final performance in Table 2 is average scaled reward, not standard navigation metrics.
results: Reward-shaped agents learn faster than plain PPO. Phi_GAT gets the best final reward on both environments (69.93 on FourRooms, 76.56 on MazeS3), beating Phi_GCN (65.28 / 66.96) and PPO (66.79 / 59.75); the gap is significant only on the harder MazeS3.
limitations: Evaluated only on two small MiniWorld environments with no standard navigation benchmarks; FourRooms differences are within std
Transition graphs are simple linear trajectory graphs without edge or graph-level features
Interpretability of attention is shown qualitatively only
